column24: An initial breeding attempt progressed into early brooding but was classified as Abandoned based on a brief occurrence of recordings containing Begging Calls followed by a rapid decline in Tricolored Blackbird vocal detections. The only Begging Calls detected for this inital attempt were 2-6kHz Nestling Begging Calls. Because the higher 6-8 kHz Hatchling Begging Calls were never detected, an estimated brooding onset was calculated by subtracting 2 days from the first date that Nestling Begging Calls were detected, which is the typical time for Hatchling Begging Calls to develop into Nestling Begging Calls. Two additional breeding attempts occurred later in the season, each characterized by a complete sequence of recordings containing Nestling Begging Calls followed by Fledgling Begging Calls. The temporal spacing and partial overlap of these breeding attempts support classification of this colony as Complex. Recordings containing Fledgling Begging Calls were detected for the latter two attempts, and each was therefore classified as Successful. The ARU deployed at this site was an LG cell phone, which produced lower-quality recordings than AudioMoth units and was prone to intermittent failure, resulting in gaps in recording coverage; while recording quality was sufficient for this analysis, direct comparisons to other datasets should be made with caution. The algorithm used to detetmine dispersal date selected a date in the middle of the weak stutter of Fledgling Begging Calls. The bulk of Fledglings left on 23 Jun, with intermittent detections of Fledgling Begging Calls continuing through the last day of recordings.

column24:
There were two ARUs deployed in this colony. This ARU had recordings from the most days and is considered the core dataset. Field visits documented a large colony that settled and initiated breeding at this site. Female Chatter detections were present initially but declined abruptly before estimated brooding onset. No Nestling or Fledgling Begging Call detections were recorded following this decline, supporting classification of the breeding attempt as Abandoned. The timing of Abandonment was temporally coincident with repeated helicopter noise detected acoustically at the site. Because no Begging Calls were detected, brooding onset was estimated as being sixteen days after Female Chatter was detected above the daily threshold, reflecting four days of nest building followed by twelve days of incubation prior to brooding onset. This difference is indicated in Table 5 with a "~".

The ARU deployed at this site was an LG cell phone, which produced lower-quality recordings than AudioMoth units and was prone to intermittent failure, resulting in gaps in recording coverage. While recording quality was sufficient for this analysis, direct comparisons to other datasets should be made with caution.

column24: Female Chatter, Nestling Begging Call, and Fledgling Begging Call detections overlapped extensively, producing a prolonged interval of mixed-stage detections characteristic of Asynchronous nesting. A careful analysis of Hatchling Begging Calls located three bouts of breeding. The spacing of these breeding bouts led to continuous Nestling and Fledgling Begging Calls. This particular colony is an example of a bout of breeding being initiated at the onset of the fledging of the prebious bout (p1n fledging and p2n incubation onsets) as well as a bout of breeding being initatied with the onset of brooding of the previous bout of breeding (p2n brooding onset coinciding with incubation onset of p3n). Recordings containing Fledgling Begging Calls were detected frequently, and the breeding attempt was therefore classified as Successful.

Female Chatter detections persisted for an extended period prior to the first detections of Nestling Begging Calls. Onset of Brooding was estimated by taking the earliest day with multiple Nestling Begging Calls detected and subtracting 2 days, the expected time for Hatchling Begging Calls to develop into Nestling Begging Calls. column24: The ARU failed shortly after the onset of brooding, preventing determination of colony type or final breeding outcome. Automated pattern matching did not detect Hatchling or Nestling Begging Calls; however, manual review identified a limited number of Nestling Begging Calls, confirming that onset of brooding had occurred. Using either the onset of Female Nest chatter +16 days or onset of earliest Nestling Begging Calls -2 days resulted in the same estimate of Brooding onset of ~6/13. Due to the lack of detections this only an approximations of the breeding dates and this is indicated with a "~". Because Nestling Begging Calls are typically detected within two days of the onset of brooding; the presence of Female Chatter detections without corresponding Nestling Begging Call detections suggests that the breeding attempt was Partially Abandoned at the time of ARU failure. Due to the equipment failure, it could not be determined whether abandonment was complete or whether any nestlings subsequently fledged. A period of prolonged extreme heat occurred immediately following brooding onset, including five consecutive days exceeding 95 °F and two days above 107 °F, and may have contributed to the outcome.

column24: Two overlapping but internally synchronous breeding cohorts were detected. Recordings containing Fledgling Begging Calls were detected for both cohorts, and both breeding attempts were therefore classified as Successful. Due to the proximity of the two breeding attempts to each other, the algorithms we used to assign dispersal for the first breeding attempt and fledgling onset for the second breeding attempt could not be used, and the dates were manually assigned. column24: Signal clarity declined after the ARU was moved from a plastic protective sleeve to a drybox. This was the first deployment using a drybox, and the reduction in recording quality was likely due to incorrect orientation of the unit within the enclosure, resulting in suboptimal alignment of the microphone with the acoustic membrane. Following this change, automated pattern matching failed to detect vocalizations. However, manual review confirmed the presence of Male Song, Female Chatter, and Begging Calls, although detected Begging Calls were likely limited to the louder Fledgling Begging Calls. Because reduced signal quality precluded reliable determination of breeding-stage transitions, no breeding-stage dates were assigned. The extended presence of Female Chatter indicates an Asynchronous colony type. Detection of Fledgling Begging Calls confirms that young successfully left the nest, and the breeding attempt was therefore classified as Successful.

column24: This deployment represents the core dataset for the Willey Wetlands colony, as it produced the highest number of recordings containing Female Chatter and Nestling Begging Call detections. This ARU was centrally located and was deployed shortly before the onset of brooding. No Male Chorus detections were recorded, indicating that chorus activity had likely ceased prior to deployment. Automated pattern matching performed well for the remaining vocalizations despite background noise from the nesting White-faced Ibis. Two ARUs were deployed at this colony. The ARU was deployed during Settlement. Male Chorus detections extended through Incubation, and Female Chatter detections persisted for several days after the onset of Brooding, patterns commonly associated with Asynchronous nesting. The temporal distribution of Begging Call detections was consistent with asynchronous breeding attempt in that Fledgling Begging Calls are heard throughout the period of fist and last expected fledging dates based of timing of Female Chatte, and Asynchronous colony type was therefore assigned. A small number of late-season recordings containing Nestling and Fledgling Begging Calls suggest the possible presence of limited additional asynchronous nesting.

Recordings containing Fledgling Begging Calls were detected, and the breeding attempt was therefore classified as Successful. A sharp decline in Fledgling Begging Call detections beginning on 18 May indicates that most fledglings dispersed at that time; however, intermittent detections continued through 31 May, suggesting that a small number of fledglings likely remained in the area after the primary dispersal event.

column24:
An initial synchronous breeding attempt was identified based on detections of Hatchling, Nestling, and Fledgling Begging Calls occurring in the expected temporal sequence. Targeted manual review for Hatchling Begging Calls during this first attempt identified three recordings on 17 May, followed by no detections on 18–19 May, coincident with a sharp increase in Male Chorus activity that likely masked these quieter vocalizations. As a result, Hatchling Begging Call detections did not meet the daily threshold for brooding onset. However, the detections on 17 May, together with the appearance of Begging Calls from older nestlings beginning on 20 May, support an estimated brooding onset of approximately 17 May. This date is therefore reported as approximate and is marked with a “~” in Table 5.

A second breeding attempt was also identified, occurring approximately 20 days after the first. Because Tricolored Blackbirds typically require at least 30 days between successive breeding attempts, this short interval indicates the arrival of an additional cohort rather than a repeat attempt by birds from the first cohort, resulting in overlapping breeding stages. Recordings containing Fledgling Begging Calls were detected for both cohorts, and each attempt was therefore classified as Successful. Due to the close temporal overlap between the two attempts, dispersal for the first attempt and fledging onset for the second could not be assigned reliably.

Following dispersal of fledglings from this initial attempt, a second breeding attempt occurred, evidenced by a temporally distinct cluster of Fledgling Begging Call detections later in the deployment. The clear temporal separation between these two fledging periods supports classification of this colony as Sequential.
During manual review of recordings associated with the second breeding attempt, Nestling Begging Calls were detected, but Hatchling Begging Calls were infrequent and did not reach the daily detection threshold. As a result, the estimated onset of brooding for this attempt is approximate and is denoted with a “~” in Table 5.
The ARI score for the second breeding attempt was zero due to the lack of Nestling Begging Call detections, a pattern that would typically indicate Abandonment. However, the presence of Fledgling Begging Call detections supports classification of this attempt as Partially Abandoned. In-person visits corroborated this interpretation and documented deterioration of the nesting substrate (milk thistle), which had become desiccated and structurally unstable and may have contributed to partial failure of the attempt. Because fledgling production was limited, Fledgling Begging Call detections were sparse and did not meet the daily threshold; consequently, fledging dates are reported as approximate and indicated with a “~” in Table 5.

The approximated dates for incubation and brooding onset are indicated with a “~” in Table 5. An ARI score of 0.333 indicates Partial Abandonment. column24:
Two ARUs were deployed at this site. The other ARU only had faint recordings, possibly due to incorrect orientation of the ARU in the drybox, so this ARU was used as the main dataset. There were a total of 3 breeding attempts. An initial breeding attempt was identified in April based on the temporal sequence of Male Chorus followed by Female Chatter. 

A second period of Male Chrous and Female Chatter began approximately 14 days later, a separation shorter than the minimum ~30-day interval between breeding attempts in Tricolored Blackbirds, indicating the arrival of an additional cohort and classification of this event as an Addition, this Addition of birds was closer to the other ARU and is not documented here and is documented at the other ARU.

A third period of Male Chorus followed by Female Chatter occurred approximately 30 days after the onset of the initial breeding attempt, consistent with a second breeding attempt by the original cohort. All breeding attempts were classified as Successful based on the presence of Fledgling Begging Calls.

This combination of Additions and Sequential breeding attempts resulted in extended overlap of breeding stages and near-continuous detections of Nestling and Fledgling Begging Calls from 10 May through ARU retrieval on 18 June. Accordingly, this colony was classified as Complex.

column24: The ARU was deployed during the incubation stage of the first of two breeding attempts. The two attempts were spaced approximately 30 days apart, consistent with Sequential colony type. Recordings containing Fledgling Begging Calls were detected for each breeding attempt, indicating that both were Successful. A small number of recordings containing Nestling and Fledgling Begging Calls were detected in July, indicating additional breeding activity; however, it is unclear whether these detections represent a small number of Asynchronous nests associated with the predominantly synchronous second attempt or a third, limited breeding attempt.

column24: Vocal detections were frequent prior to 13 June, after which detections declined sharply. A small fraction of recordings contained Fledgling Begging Calls detections, indicating that some young successfully left the nest. The ARI score for this breeding attempt was 0.113, corresponding to classification as Partially Abandoned. The abrupt reduction in detections shortly after the onset of brooding was temporally coincident with a heat event and may have contributed to the Partial Abandonment. column2: 2024 Dublin Ranch Preserve - Lin Livermore Conservation Area
column23: Approximately 4500 sq. meter stock pond within a ~400 acre grassland matrix that also hosts California Red-legged Frog, California Tiger Salamander, and seasonal waterfowl. Surrounding land uses are ranching and horse boarding. There is a shooting range nearby.
column24:
In-person visits documented settlement behavior on 15 May and incubation on 21 May. The ARU was deployed on 21 May, and the onset of brooding was acoustically determined to be 31 May, consistent with field observations. Recordings containing Fledgling Begging Calls were detected during incubation and likely originated from fledglings produced during a prior breeding attempt. Subsequent Fledgling Begging Call detections in mid-June indicate that the breeding attempt recorded by this ARU was classified as Successful. A small number of late Fledgling Begging Call detections following dispersal of most fledglings indicate the presence of a small number of asynchronous nests.
The site had been labeled 2024 Dublin Ranch Preserve - Lin Livermore Conservation Area, but was renamed to align with data from prior years.

column23: A patch of Himalayan blackberry about 900 sq m that is just uphill from a 200 sq m small pond. Surrounding this area is open grassland with grazing cattle.
column24:
Early-season activity was characterized by sustained Male Chorus detections throughout March and April, followed by fewer Female Chatter detections. Vocal detections declined abruptly on 25 April, shortly after the onset of incubation. The ARI score for this breeding attempt was 0.00 due to the absence of Nestling Begging Call detections, a pattern that would ordinarily indicate Abandonment; however, a small fraction of recordings contained Fledgling Begging Call detections, supporting classification as Partially Abandoned. An in-person site visit on 29 April corroborated this classification.
During this period, two sources of disturbance were documented. Feral pig vocalizations were detected in eleven recordings between 24 March and 1 April, and site visits confirmed their presence in the nesting substrate; pigs were removed by 15 April. Coyote vocalizations were detected in five recordings between 29 March and 7 May, and site visits documented their presence near the colony from 29 April to 24 June. Although these disturbances may have contributed to the Partial Abandonment of the first breeding attempt, Male Chorus and Female Chatter detections persisted during the period of pig activity, and the Partial Abandonment occurred approximately ten days after pig removal, suggesting that feral pigs alone were not the primary driver. It is possible that access paths created in the nesting substrate facilitated predator access to nests. Due to the Partial Abandonment, detections of Fledgling Begging Calls were sparse and did not meet the daily threshold, and while there is evidence to support reporting a few successful fledglings, there are not enough detections to determine dates of onset or dispersal.
A second breeding attempt was initiated later in the season and progressed through fledging. A marked increase in Fledgling Begging Call detections on 21 June likely corresponds to the fledging date for this second attempt, which was classified as Successful.

column23: A weedy field with mustard and milk thistle next to an almond orchard. Birds were travelling from the nearby dairies to the field. There were seasonal wetlands near the colony that the birds also used for foraging and sources of mud. Corn was planted about 60 meters away from the colony during the beginning of the nesting attempts. The ARU was placed on the side of the colony, near the densest cluster.
column24: Signal clarity was reduced throughout the deployment, and spectrograms revealed a persistent 2kHz band of Male Chorus, indicating presence of a colony beyond the effective recording range of the ARU. As a result, automated pattern matching detected only a limited number of recordings containing Female Chatter and no Nestling Begging Call detections, necessitating manual review. Presence of Fledgling Begging Calls indicate Successful breeding. Pattern of Male Chorus and Fledgling Begging Calls are consistent with multiple bouts of breeding. An interprestation consistent with these results would be bout 1 Incubation Onset 4/21, Breeding Onset 5/3, Fledging Onset 5/17 (based on a handful of Fledgling Begging Calls starting on 5/17) and bout 2 Iincunation Onset 5/1, Brooding Onset 5/13, Fledging Onset 5/27 (based on Male Chorus bout ending on 5/1 and sharp increase in Fledgling Begging Calls seen on 5/27), and bout 3 Incubation Onset 5/27, Begging Onset 6/7, Fledging Onset 6/21 (based on Male Chorus end of 5/27 and a small Fledgling Begging Call block on 6/21) which would be consistent with Incubation Onest for additional breeding bouts tending to coincide with either Brooding Onset or Fledging Onset. However while the data are consistent, they are too sparse for confident assignments of breeding dates. Backyard pond choked with cattails, 40X125 meters in size. Two residences under renovation, fenced lot, a few trees and limited shrubbery around the pond. Sparse desert scrub (Atriplex polycarpa dominant, Larrea tridentata co-dominant) in all directions with a few scattered homes. column24: The ARU was deployed for seven days. Recordings containing Fledgling Begging Calls were detected during the deployment, and the breeding attempt was therefore classified as Successful. column23: Stock-pond within a conservation easement. Pond sits below a residence with driveway running along it's western side (offset 120 ft).
column24:
Female Chatter detections overlapped extensively with Nestling and Fledgling Begging Call detections, indicating Asynchronous colony type. Rainfall occurred during early brooding but was not associated with a reduction in vocal detections. Sustained Fledgling Begging Call detections indicate that young successfully left the nest, and the breeding attempt was therefore classified as Successful. The algorithm detected that there was a Fledgling Dispersal event on 5/28 suggesting that a large portion of the fledglings left on this date. There are two additional breeding pulses that have a small number of supporting Begging Call detections. Male Chorus was not associated with either of these two pulses, though an increase in the dectection of Male Song correlates with these two additional bouts of breeding.  
The site had been labeled 2024 Ohlone - Santa Lucia Preserve, but was renamed to align with naming patterns of other sites.

column2: 2024 Panoche Creek Preserve - Dollar Marsh East
column23: A series of tule stands in a dynamic riparian system along Panoche Creek, up to about 2.0 miles upstream from Panoche Road. The creek is lined with a combination of cattails and bulrushes with sparse willows and large cottonwoods interspersed.  The suitability of the cattails and bulrushes as nesting substrate varies from year to year.
column24:
Field visits documented a large colony at this site. Three ARUs were deployed, and the unit located on the eastern side of the site produced the greatest number of recordings containing vocalizations and therefore serves as the core dataset for this colony. The dominant detection pattern was consistent with a Simple synchronous breeding attempt. However, a small subset of recordings containing Female Chatter after the onset of Brooding, together with extended detections of Nestling and Fledgling Begging Calls, suggests the presence of limited asynchronous nesting within the colony. Because the overall detection pattern indicates that most nesting activity followed a synchronous trajectory, the colony was classified as Simple.

A small number of recordings containing Female Chatter were also detected in early June (11 recordings across a 12-day period), suggesting the possibility of a second breeding attempt; however, no temporally associated Fledgling Begging Call detections were recorded, and due to the lack of detections in general for this breesing attempt and the presence and outcome of a second attempt could not be confirmed.

column23: NEED
column24: Two ARUs were deployed at this colony; this dataset was designated as the core dataset because it contained a higher number of detections. An initial breeding attempt was detected primarily through recordings containing through Male Chrous and Female Chatter. Hatchling and Nestling Begging Calls were not detected during this first attempt. If an estimate of expected Incubation Onset is done using Female Chatter (Incubation Onset =Female Chatter onset +4) its estimate is ~4/13, Incubation Onset ~4/25, and Fledgling Onset ~5/7. The first block of FBC is on 5/19, which is much later than expected, and there fore it is uncertain if these fledglings are associated with this breeding attempt. One interpretation is that the birds that attempted to breed that were vocally recorded abandoned their attempt. The FBC that are later picked up are from a successful breeding attempt that was outside of the range of the recorder, and these fledglings are actually a dispersed creche from another location. Because of this uncertainity the breeding outcome of this first pulse has been marked as Unknown. Approximately one month later, a second breeding attempt began and continued through fledging and dispersal. Detection patterns indicate that this second attempt was Asynchronous. Because the colony exhibited both Sequential and Asynchronous breeding patterns, it was classified as Complex. Recordings containing Fledgling Begging Calls were detected for both attempts, and both were classified as Successful.

column23: Birds nested in a milk thistle patch northwest of the Bridge Street Pond and near Mystic Lake. A nearby dairy farm is a source for foraging. Thistle patch surrounded on three sides by rank weedy vegetation, notably Pepperweed (Lepidium latifolium) and Sow Thistle (Sonchus sp.) with patches of Mulefat (Baccharis salicifolius) .  To the east is the Mystic Lake shoreline.
column24: Nestling Begging Call detections were present in the earliest recordings, indicating that the ARU was deployed during brooding. This was a small colony, resulting in infrequent vocalization detections. A mini manual analysis from 10-Jun to 15-Jun revealed that Nestling Begging Calls were faily abundant through 10-Jun and then declined to nearly nothing. In-person visits noted that the Flgdglings had dispersed to a nearby location, suggesting that the Fledglings dispersed immediately and moved to this other substrate that was out of reach of the ARU detection. A handful of Fledgling Begging Calls were detected, and the in-person visits confirm that the colony was Successful.

column23: Cottonwoods partly encircling the colony wetland
column24:
Only a small fraction of recordings contained Tricolored Blackbird vocalization detections, consistent with the small colony documented at this site. Despite sparse detections, two temporally distinct intervals of recordings containing Female Chatter followed by Fledgling Begging Call detections, separated by approximately 30 days, support inference of two discrete synchronous breeding attempts. Recordings containing Fledgling Begging Calls were detected for both attempts, and each was therefore classified as Successful.
Breeding-stage dates were assigned based on the first detected vocalizations; however, because detections were sparse, the true onset of breeding stages likely occurred earlier and reported dates should be considered approximate. This is indicated with a "~" in Table 5.

column23: Surrounded by wetlands, common reed, weedy fields, crop, ranchland and shrub steppe
column24: Although Male Chorus was not reliably detected, Hatchling, Nestling, and Fledgling Begging Calls were detected. An ARI score of 0.283 indicates Partial Abandonment. Detections of Fledgling Begging Calls extended through late May, indicating that although the colony was Partially Abandoned, a portion of nests successfully produced fledglings. Due to the Partial Abandonment, detections of Fledgling Begging Calls were sparse and did not meet the daily threshold, and so the reported dates are approximate. This is indicated with a "~" in Table 5.

column23: A 16-acre wetland comprised mainly of stinging nettle
column24:
Nestling and Fledgling Begging Call detections were present in the earliest recordings, indicating that breeding had begun prior to ARU deployment. Continued overlap of Nestling and Fledgling Begging Call detections supports classification of this colony as Asynchronous. The algorithm detected a stronger block of Fledgling Begging Calls starting 5/27, suggesting a second pulse of breeding is embedded in the Asynchronous breeding, however there is not a block of Male Chorus, Female Chatter, Hatchling, or Nestling Begging calls associated with it. A review of recordings around the expected onset of Brooding also failed to locate any Hatchling Begging Calls. This could be due to the Asynchronous nature of the first pulse overlapping the second pulse that this block of Fledgling Begging Calls may represent. Therefore the theoretical second bout of breeding dates for Incubation Onset, and Breeding Onset are inferred from this block of Fledgling Begging Calls which is indicated with a "~".

column23: Seasonal creek with stinging nettle, cattails and grasses
column24: Two distinct breeding attempts were found, characterized by extended Female Chatter detections and overlapping Begging Call detections, indicating Asynchronous nesting within each attempt. The resulting prolonged presence of Fledgling Begging Call detections reflects overlap between attempts. Both breeding attempts progressed through fledging and dispersal and were classified as Successful.

column23: A 5-acre wetland comprised of stinging nettle, cattails, mule fat and willows
column24: Nestling and Fledgling Begging Call detections were present from the first day of recording, indicating that breeding was already underway prior to ARU deployment. Extended overlap of Nestling and Fledgling Begging Call detections indicates a continuous breeding pattern consistent with an Asynchronous colony structure. Fledgling Begging Call detections persisted through late June, and the breeding attempt was therefore classified as Successful.

column23: A 1/4- acre wetland, derived from a nearby spring, comprised of stinging nettle
column24: Hatchling Begging Call detections were recorded on the first day of recording, indicating that the onset of brooding occurred shortly before ARU deployment. Nestling Begging Call detections were followed by Fledgling Begging Call detections in the expected temporal order for a Simple synchronous colony, and a subsequent abrupt decline in fledgling detections marks dispersal. The breeding attempt was therefore classified as Successful.
